finding.claim: Unvalidated callbackUrl from POST /subscribe is stored and later used as the target of a server-side POST, enabling blind SSRF to internal or metadata endpoints.
finding.source: callbackUrl request body field, passed to subscribe() at Jobs.java:13
finding.sink: client.send(req, ...) at Jobs.java:24 after URI.create(cb) at Jobs.java:21

trace.note: subscribe(name, callbackUrl) accepts the value without validation
Value stored unchanged in static subscriptions map
notifyAll iterates over all stored callback values; runs periodically per comment at line 17
HttpClient sends a POST with the payload to the attacker-chosen URI

finding.guards_checked: No scheme allowlist, no host allowlist, no private/loopback/link-local/metadata IP blocking, no DNS pinning. HttpClient.newHttpClient() defaults to Redirect.NEVER, so redirect-based bypass does not apply. Response body is discarded, so the attacker cannot read it directly (blind). Route auth guard for /subscribe is not in this repo and could not be verified. Whether the attacker controls the POST payload depends on the notifyAll caller, which is not in this repo.

verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: subscribe() stores callbackUrl unchanged at src/Jobs.java:14, notifyAll() calls URI.create(cb) and client.send() at lines 21 and 24, and no validation exists anywhere in the repo. Whether a remote attacker can reach subscribe() is not decidable here, because the only evidence is the comment at src/Jobs.java:12 and the POST /subscribe route handler and its auth guard are not in this repo, so an admin-only or authenticated-admin route would refute the finding.
